headline: Museums branch out into hotels and virtual reality

sources.title: From hotel suites to virtual reality, museums turn to licensing deals as costs rise (The Guardian)
Park Plaza London Riverbank Launches Natural History Museum Dinosaur Family Suite (Hospitality & Catering News)
Sandbox VR's Prehistoric Immersive Experience AGE OF DINOSAURS Roars into Locations Around the Globe on 3 April (Total Licensing)

chunks.text: Many museums in Britain are [[free to visit]], but they still need money. Now some are {{branching out}} into hotels, fashion and virtual reality. They use [[licensing deals]], which let other companies use a museum's name and [[collections]]. Families can now check into a London hotel [[suite]] designed with the Natural History Museum. The children's room has a [[bunk bed]] with a T. rex design. A night there starts at 724 pounds.

verbs.correct: To start doing new kinds of things
verbs.why: Many chefs branch out into new kinds of food after a few years. Photographers often branch out into video. Some British museums are branching out into hotels, fashion and virtual reality.

chunks.text: Museums face [[funding cuts]] and [[rising costs]], so they need new ways to {{bring in}} money. The Natural History Museum says its licensing program grows by about 15 percent a year. Experiences {{make up}} a growing part of it. The museum also {{teamed up}} with a virtual reality company on an adventure called Age of Dinosaurs, which opened in April. Players {{put on}} special vests to feel the [[footsteps]] of giant dinosaurs.

verbs.why: A school bake sale often brings in a few hundred dollars. Her second job brings in a little extra each month. Museums face funding cuts and rising costs, so they need new ways to bring in money.

verbs.correct: To form a part of something
verbs.why: Online orders make up half of the store's sales. Children make up most of the swimmers at the pool. Experiences make up a growing part of the Natural History Museum's licensing program.
Local bakeries often team up to share costs. Neighbors team up to clean the park each spring. The Natural History Museum teamed up with a virtual reality company on Age of Dinosaurs.

Most people put on a jacket before they go outside. Many diners put on their glasses to read the menu. In Age of Dinosaurs, players put on special vests so they can feel the footsteps of giant dinosaurs.

chunks.text: Other museums are doing the same. The British Museum worked with a London [[department store]] on products based on a famous old tapestry. Some of them {{ended up}} in Vogue magazine. The Victoria and Albert Museum {{rolled out}} 63 [[product lines]] in 2025. It wants new ways to {{draw on}} its collection of 2.8 million objects. One line is phone cases. Another puts its [[artwork]] on a television that shows pictures when it is {{turned off}}.

verbs.wrong: To be sold at a low price
verbs.why: Lost suitcases often end up in the wrong city. Drivers who take a wrong turn often end up in a small town. Some of the British Museum's tapestry products ended up in Vogue magazine.

verbs.wrong: To test a product in secret
verbs.why: Phone companies roll out cheaper plans every year. Coffee chains roll out new menus each fall. The Victoria and Albert Museum rolled out 63 product lines in 2025.

verbs.correct: To use something as a source
verbs.wrong: To close a gallery for repairs
verbs.why: Writers often draw on their own childhood for novels. Good teachers draw on many years of experience. The Victoria and Albert Museum wants new ways to draw on its collection of 2.8 million objects.

verbs.correct: To make a machine stop working
verbs.why: Most people turn off the TV before bed. Many students turn off their laptops to save the battery. One of the museum's product lines puts artwork on a television that shows pictures when it is turned off.

chunks.text: The money is growing fast. An [[industry group]] says sales of licensed products and services in Britain grew 7 percent in 2025, to 19.2 billion dollars. Sales in the [[category]] that includes museums grew by more than 8 percent. A category that includes [[immersive experiences]] {{shot up}} by 53 percent. In early October 2026, more museums than before went to a big licensing [[conference]] in London. There, they {{took on}} big TV [[brands]] such as Harry Potter for attention.

verbs.why: Gas prices often shoot up after a big storm. The number of beach visitors shoots up in July. Sales in a category that includes immersive experiences shot up by 53 percent in 2025.

verbs.wrong: To share a booth with someone
verbs.why: Our small team takes on the state champions every year. New coffee shops often take on big chains for customers. At a licensing conference in London in October 2026, museums took on big TV brands such as Harry Potter for attention.

mainIdea.s: British museums use licensing deals to earn money from hotels, virtual reality and products. They face funding cuts and rising costs, and this business is growing fast.
mainIdea.why: Museums let companies use their names and collections to bring in money. Sales in this market grew in 2025, and immersive experiences rose by 53 percent.

mainIdea.s: Some London museums now sell old objects from their collections to hotels and game makers. Their ticket sales have dropped, so they need the cash to stay open for visitors.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the museums are not selling objects. They let other companies use their names and collections, and many of them are free to visit.

mainIdea.s: A large London museum will close for two years while builders repair its old roof. During the work, its dinosaur fossils will travel to smaller museums around the country.
mainIdea.why: No museum is closing. Museums are branching out into hotels, virtual reality and products through licensing deals.

tf.s: Some museums are branching out into hotels, fashion and virtual reality.
tf.why: Families can now stay in a London hotel suite designed with the Natural History Museum, and players can join a dinosaur adventure.

tf.s: Museums refuse to let other companies use their names and collections.

tf.s: Players in Age of Dinosaurs put on special vests to feel dinosaur footsteps.
tf.why: The vests let players feel the footsteps of giant dinosaurs as they move through the adventure.

tf.s: The Victoria and Albert Museum stopped making products from its collection.
tf.why: It rolled out many new product lines in 2025 and wants new ways to draw on its collection.

tf.s: Museums are branching out because their funding has increased.
tf.why: They face funding cuts and rising costs, so they need new ways to bring in money.

tf.s: Money from licensed products and services in Britain is growing fast.
tf.why: Sales grew in 2025, and a category that includes immersive experiences shot up.

lines.text: Did you know you can sleep in a dinosaur room at a London hotel now?
Really? Does a museum have something to do with it?
Yes. The Natural History Museum {{teamed up}} with the hotel. The kids' bunk bed has a T. rex design.
Kids would love that. What does it cost?
It starts at 724 pounds a night.
Wow. That's [[a far cry from]] buying a T-shirt in the gift shop.
Right. Museums are {{branching out}} because they need to {{bring in}} more money.
Why? Aren't a lot of them free?
They are, but they face funding cuts and rising costs. These deals help [[keep the lights on]].
Well, [[money is tight]] everywhere. What else are they doing?
The same museum made a virtual reality adventure too. You {{put on}} a special vest and feel the dinosaurs walking.
Now that's [[right up my alley]]. Are other museums doing this?
Yes. The Victoria and Albert Museum {{rolled out}} 63 product lines in 2025, like phone cases.
Is it really that big a business?
Sales in the category that includes immersive experiences {{shot up}} 53 percent in 2025.
That's huge. I might book that dinosaur suite with my nephew. For a kid who loves dinosaurs, it's [[worth every penny]].

expressions.def: Used to say that one thing is very different from another
ex: This hotel is a far cry from the cheap motel we stayed in last year.

expressions.def: Used about earning just enough money to keep a place running
ex: The theater sells snacks to keep the lights on.

expressions.def: Used to say that there is not much money to spend
ex: Money is tight this month, so we are eating at home.
When money is tight, the city cuts library hours.

expressions.def: Used to say something expensive is good enough to justify its price
ex: The new mattress cost a lot, but it was worth every penny.
Our family trip to the lake was worth every penny.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is exactly the kind of thing you like
ex: A cooking class in Italy? That's right up my alley.
Old movies are right up my alley.
